claims.text: Tungsten particles should be coated with an ultrathin, uniform copper layer before consolidation.
Pre-coating tungsten particles with copper will improve tungsten–copper interfacial bonding.
The copper coating will reduce conduction-electron scattering at tungsten–copper interfaces.
Reduced interfacial electron scattering will increase the composite's thermal conductivity.
The copper-coated W–Cu composite will retain mechanical durability comparable to an otherwise identical composite containing uncoated tungsten.
The copper-coated W–Cu composite will retain irradiation resistance comparable to an otherwise identical composite containing uncoated tungsten.
Fusion-facing materials encounter high-temperature and intense irradiation conditions, including energetic-neutron exposure.
Thermal cycling at 300–500 °C, irradiation, and concurrent mechanical loading are representative conditions for W–Cu fusion-reactor joints.
Copper-coated tungsten particles will form a seamless, compositionally compatible interphase with the copper matrix.
The copper interphase will alleviate lattice-structure and work-function mismatches at the tungsten–copper boundary.
Alleviating interfacial mismatches will reduce interfacial thermal resistance.
The copper interphase will facilitate electronic transport between the copper matrix and tungsten inclusions.
Introducing the copper interphase will not alter the reinforcing microstructure responsible for mechanical durability.
The reinforcing microstructure of the W–Cu composite imparts irradiation tolerance.
The conductivity benefit requires a uniformly thin copper coating on the order of tens of nanometers.
An excessively thick copper coating could introduce undesirable intermetallic phases or compromise particle–matrix bonding.
The predicted benefit requires the copper coating to remain intact under irradiation.
The optimum copper-coating thickness and deposition method remain to be determined experimentally.
The long-term stability of the copper interphase under fusion-relevant irradiation remains unvalidated.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant conductivity increase, or degradation of durability or irradiation resistance beyond an acceptable margin, would falsify the hypothesis.
